opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. Generalization in multiphysics is a hard problem, and I think it helps to separate a few different kinds of generalization, because people tend to lump them together.

The first is generalization across resolution and discretization. That was a big motivation for neural operators. If you learn a mapping between function spaces rather than between fixed grids, you can train on coarse data and evaluate at finer resolutions, or move between different meshes. That kind of generalization is more achievable because it is built into the architecture rather than hoped for from the data.

The second is generalization across parameters within a family of physics: different Reynolds numbers, boundary conditions, material properties, geometries. Here the model can interpolate well when training covers the regime, but extrapolation is where things break. Turbulence is a classic example. Moving into a regime with qualitatively different dynamics, new instabilities, new scales interacting, means you are asking the model to infer something it has never seen evidence of.

The third, and the hardest, is generalization across physics itself, which is what people mean by multiphysics foundation models. Can one model trained on fluids, elasticity, and electromagnetics transfer to a coupled problem it wasn't trained on? I think there is real promise, because many PDEs share structure: conservation laws, diffusion, advection, wave propagation. A model can learn reusable building blocks. But coupling is where emergent behavior lives. Fluid-structure interaction or magnetohydrodynamics isn't just the sum of its parts, and the interfaces between physical regimes are where purely data-driven models struggle most.

So my view is that the limits are set mainly by two things. One is data coverage, because high-fidelity simulation data is expensive and we will never cover every regime. The other is the lack of inductive biases that enforce physical consistency. That is why I'm a strong advocate of combining data with physics. For example, adding PDE residual losses at test time or during fine-tuning lets the model correct itself in regimes where data is sparse. You get the speed of a learned surrogate with a constraint that keeps it honest.

Uncertainty quantification is equally important. In science and engineering, a model that is wrong and confident is dangerous. We need models that can say "I'm outside my training distribution," so you can fall back to a numerical solver or collect more data in that regime. That kind of active, closed-loop setup, where the AI and the traditional solver work together, is where I think the practical path to robust generalization lies.

So I'm optimistic, but I don't think scale alone gets us there the way it has in language. Physics gives us structure we would be foolish not to use.

r001.rationale: The response says that unfamiliar dynamics leave the model without evidence to infer from, but does not state that transfer is impossible when a phenomenon is completely unseen.

r002.rationale: It describes reusable building blocks learned across physics, but does not say that prior learning reduces the number of fine-tuning examples needed for coupled behavior.

r003.rationale: It says coupled physics is not simply the sum of its parts and that interfaces can challenge data-driven models, but does not identify highly nonlinear coupling or the need for additional training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the way I think about it is that generalization in multiphysics is really a question of what the model has actually learned: the operator, or just the data.

When we started working on neural operators, the whole motivation was that classical neural networks learn mappings between finite-dimensional vectors, but physics lives in function spaces. A PDE solution operator maps an initial condition, a function, to a solution, another function. If you learn in that space, you get properties like discretization invariance, so you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another, and you get zero-shot super-resolution. That's a form of generalization that a standard CNN or transformer on a fixed grid simply doesn't have.

But I want to be honest about where the limits are. There are really three axes.

The first is distribution shift in the inputs. If you train a Fourier neural operator on Navier-Stokes at one Reynolds number and ask it about a regime that's much more turbulent, you're asking it to extrapolate into dynamics it has never seen. The operator framing helps, but it's not magic. Physics has regime changes, bifurcations, phase transitions, and data-driven models struggle at those boundaries unless you build in the structure.

The second axis is coupling. Multiphysics means you have, say, fluid flow coupled to heat transfer coupled to structural deformation, and the interesting phenomena come from the interactions. A model that learned each physics in isolation won't automatically generalize to the coupled system, because the coupling introduces new time scales and new invariants. This is where I think we need to be much more deliberate about architecture: you want latent representations that respect conservation laws across the coupled subsystems, not just within each one.

The third is geometry. Real engineering problems don't live on nice periodic boxes. Our work on geometry-informed neural operators was motivated by exactly this. If you want a model that generalizes from one car body to another, or one aircraft wing to another, it has to understand the geometry as an input, not something baked into the training set.

So how do we push the limits? I'm a big believer in putting physics back in. Physics-informed losses, enforcing symmetries, using the PDE residual as a constraint. In the weather work, for example, FourCastNet generalized remarkably well on forecasting, but we know that's because the atmosphere is sampled densely and the dynamics are well covered in reanalysis data. In regimes where you're data-poor, you need the equations to fill the gap.

The honest answer is that these models are tremendously good at interpolation in a very high-dimensional sense, including across resolutions and geometries, and they are not yet reliable for extrapolating into new physical regimes. I think the path forward is hybrid: neural operators as fast surrogates inside loops where you still have a numerical solver or physical constraints checking the result, and increasingly, foundation models that have seen many physics so that fewer things are truly out of distribution.

r001.rationale: The response says models are not yet reliable when extrapolating into new physical regimes, but does not state that transfer is impossible when a phenomenon is completely unseen.

r002.rationale: It says models trained on individual physics will not automatically generalize to coupled systems, but does not say prior learning reduces the number of fine-tuning examples needed.

r003.rationale: The response notes that coupling introduces new time scales and invariants, but does not identify highly nonlinear coupling or additional training as the reason familiar phenomena may fail to combine.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: generalization to what? A new geometry, a different boundary condition, a new range of material properties, or a regime where different physics becomes dominant? Those are very different challenges, and good performance on one doesn’t establish the others.

In multiphysics, the coupling is especially important. You might have models that work well for fluid flow and heat transfer individually, but once you couple them, small errors can feed back and grow. So you need to evaluate the coupled system, including its stability over time, rather than just the accuracy of each component.

Physical structure can help constrain the learning problem—conservation laws, symmetries, boundary conditions—but it doesn’t guarantee that the model will extrapolate to a new regime. If you cross a transition where the behavior changes qualitatively, that’s a much stronger test than interpolating among familiar examples.

So I would think of these models as having a domain of validity that we need to characterize. The goal is not just to make predictions, but to identify when those predictions need additional simulation or experimental validation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses extrapolation limits and new regimes, but does not say transfer is impossible when a physical phenomenon is completely unseen.

r002.rationale: It says coupling can amplify errors, but does not state that learning individual phenomena reduces the examples needed to fine-tune a coupled model.

r003.rationale: It notes that coupled errors can feed back and grow, but does not identify highly nonlinear coupling as a reason familiar phenomena may fail to combine without additional training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: generalization with respect to what? You might change the initial conditions, the geometry, the material properties, or even the coupling between different physical processes. Those are very different challenges, and doing well on one doesn’t establish that you can handle the others.

With multiphysics, a particular challenge is that the coupling can introduce behavior you haven’t seen in the individual systems. You can have a good model of each component and still get the combined dynamics wrong, especially when processes operate at very different scales.

So I think incorporating physics is essential: conservation laws, symmetries, and the structure of the governing equations give you constraints beyond the training data. But they don’t guarantee extrapolation. You still need to test across physical regimes, understand where errors accumulate, and identify when the model is outside its range of validity. That’s where combining learned models with numerical solvers can be very powerful.

r001.rationale: The response says coupling may produce behavior not seen in individual systems, but it does not state that transfer is impossible when the target phenomenon is completely unseen.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss reducing the number of fine-tuning examples by learning individual phenomena first.

r003.rationale: It says coupling can make combined dynamics hard to model, but does not identify highly nonlinear coupling or say additional training is needed.
